title: Attention span, history not being sexy, and mentoring younger musicians
summary: Jang talks about audiences' short attention, the stickiness of stories, Art Blakey hiring younger players, and being mentored by Max Roach.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Have you noticed, we also had talked a little bit about people’s attention span. And this was ten years ago. And now things have — the demands on our attention, multi-tasking etcetera, have greatly increased. Does that affect your audience do you think? Are they affected by that?

Well you’re interviewing me. I can’t lay out this long history. Because history is not sexy. And we had spoke about Malcolm Gladwell’s A Tipping Point. There has to be a stickiness. And you have to sort of go for it, and then we are also living in a highly competitive economic society and people don’t have the time, they’re overscheduled and you really have to like — it’s almost like being in New York in the zoo. You’ve got to — no matter if you lay out your best shot, it may not be embraced, you may not get that opportunity, etcetera, etcetera. So having this opportunity to be interviewed I can speak more freely and at length, but yes, if I’m in a live performance there’s just a lot of different aspects that I have to reconsider. So I don’t perform as much but it seems like in some ways I feel a loyalty to the artists that have developed my music. But then I understand in a certain sense why Art Blakey had — well from my perspective, not from Art Blakey’s — when he started to hire younger musicians. I mean part of it is transmission — trying to nurture the younger generation. But partly it is also bringing younger audiences to the concerts. So I think now I have to — I’ll have to consider that but what’s difficult is why would young artists want to hang socially with an old guy like me? And then I guess I shouldn’t really criticize or put myself down because hey, for me, being with — I mean I was mentored by Max Roach. He was the age of my father. Max Roach was like a father figure. I’m not sure if that — well maybe I don’t think highly enough of myself, but I’m not sure — well yeah, maybe I could play that role. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-
